chunks.title: Ptosis: don't miss list & types
chunks.tldr: Rule out the dangerous ones: Horner, III nerve palsy, myasthenia, orbital/lid tumour, CPEO (Kearns–Sayre). Types: aponeurotic (commonest; high crease, good levator 10–15 mm, worse in downgaze), myogenic/congenital (poor levator 0–5 mm, no crease), neurogenic, mechanical, traumatic, pseudoptosis. Always document pupils + motility.
points: Aponeurotic causes: ageing, rubbing, RGP lens handling, trauma, intraocular surgery (speculum).
Horner: ~2 mm upper + lower lid 'reverse ptosis'.
Marcus Gunn jaw-wink: lid rises with jaw movement.
Pseudoptosis: contralateral retraction/proptosis, enophthalmos, hypertropia, dermatochalasis, brow ptosis.
Measure MRD1, levator function (block frontalis), crease, Hertel, lagophthalmos, Bell, fatigue, palpate superior orbit.
Young + ptosis + ophthalmoplegia → dilate for pigmentary retinopathy → urgent ECG (KSS heart block).
Tests: ice test (MG), phenylephrine 2.5% (predicts Müller resection response).
Every III nerve palsy (pupil-sparing too) → urgent CTA/MRA; Horner → head + neck imaging (dissection), chest CT.
chunks.hook: Ptosis + big pupil = III; + small pupil = Horner; + fatigue = MG.

cards.q: Levator function in aponeurotic vs congenital myogenic ptosis?
cards.a: Aponeurotic: good (10–15 mm). Congenital myogenic: poor (0–5 mm).

cards.q: Purpose of the phenylephrine test in ptosis?
cards.a: Lid elevation after 2.5% phenylephrine predicts good outcome with Müller muscle–conjunctival resection.

chunks.title: Ptosis management
chunks.tldr: Treat cause. Non-surgical: observe, tape, lid crutches. Surgery: levator advancement (good function), frontalis sling (poor function), Müllerectomy/Fasanella–Servat (mild, phenylephrine-responsive). Congenital: watch amblyopia (occlusion or astigmatism). Traumatic: wait 6 months.
points: Postop: infection, bleeding, exposure, asymmetry; mild lagophthalmos 2–3 weeks normal.
Poor Bell/lagophthalmos → under-correct to protect cornea.
chunks.hook: Good levator → advance it. No levator → borrow frontalis.

cards.q: Surgery for ptosis with poor levator function?

chunks.title: Chalazion & hordeolum
chunks.tldr: Chalazion = blocked meibomian/Zeis gland, firm lump. Hordeolum = acute staph abscess (external Zeis / internal meibomian). Rx: warm compresses + massage q.i.d., short antibiotic (hordeolum) or antibiotic-steroid ointment (chalazion), doxycycline if recurrent/rosacea. Persisting 3–4 weeks → I&C or intralesional triamcinolone. Recurrent chalazion in older patient → biopsy (sebaceous carcinoma).
points: Steroid injection risks: skin depigmentation/atrophy (dark skin), rare retinal artery occlusion.
Worsening hordeolum → I&D, treat as preseptal cellulitis.
DDx: preseptal cellulitis, forniceal FB, pyogenic granuloma.
Send all excised atypical/recurrent lesions for histology.
chunks.hook: Same spot, again and again, in an older person = biopsy it.

cards.q: Risk of intralesional steroid for chalazion in dark skin?

chunks.title: Ectropion, entropion & trichiasis
chunks.tldr: Ectropion: involutional (laxity, commonest), paralytic (VII — wait 3–6 months), cicatricial, mechanical, allergic, congenital. Entropion: involutional, cicatricial (pemphigoid, SJS, trachoma, burns), spastic (Quickert suture), congenital. Trichiasis: epilate few lashes; recurrent → electrolysis/cryo/RF/laser/surgery; distichiasis; epiblepharon (Asian kids).
points: Lubricate exposed cornea; tape lids as temporary fix.
VII palsy + hearing loss → image for acoustic neuroma.
Evert lids in trichiasis to look for scarring/symblepharon.
Prostaglandin drops can cause trichiasis.

cards.q: Bedside temporary fix for spastic lower lid entropion?

cards.a: An extra row of lashes emerging from meibomian gland orifices.

chunks.title: Floppy eyelid syndrome
chunks.tldr: Obese (often male) patient, chronic red irritated eyes worse on waking; upper lid everts with a gentle pull, rubbery tarsus, papillae. Linked to obstructive sleep apnoea, keratoconus, Down. Rx: ointment, tape/shield at night, don't sleep face-down; lateral tarsal strip/wedge resection. Refer for sleep study.
points: Unilateral if they sleep on that side.
OSA matters for anaesthesia before surgery.
chunks.hook: Lid flips by itself → ask about snoring.

cards.q: Systemic association to check in floppy eyelid syndrome?

chunks.title: Blepharospasm & mimics
chunks.tldr: Bilateral involuntary orbicularis spasm, gone in sleep; + jaw/neck = Meige. Rx: treat surface irritation, botulinum toxin, myectomy if fails. Hemifacial spasm: one side, persists in sleep → MRI CP angle. Myokymia: harmless lid twitch (caffeine, stress). Also Tourette, tardive dyskinesia, apraxia of lid opening (Parkinson — can't open, no spasm).
points: Typical blepharospasm needs no imaging.
Lorazepam/methylphenidate occasionally.
chunks.hook: Both eyes = blepharospasm. One face side = hemifacial (scan).

cards.q: Key difference between hemifacial spasm and blepharospasm?
cards.a: Hemifacial is unilateral, involves the whole half-face and persists during sleep; needs MRI of CP angle.

chunks.title: Canaliculitis
chunks.tldr: Pouting red punctum, nasal-sided recurrent conjunctivitis, gritty concretions on expression. Actinomyces (sulphur granules); also retained punctal plug. Rx: express/canaliculotomy to remove stones, irrigate with antibiotic, topical + oral antibiotics (doxycycline), warm compresses; fungus → nystatin.
points: DDx: dacryocystitis (sac swelling), chalazion, NLDO.
Ask about previous plugs.

chunks.title: Dacryocystitis
chunks.tldr: Tender red swelling below the medial canthal tendon, pus from punctum on pressure; due to NLDO. Swelling above the tendon → think tumour. Rx: systemic antibiotics (co-amoxiclav/cephalexin; MRSA → TMP-SMX/clindamycin; sick → IV), warm massage, drain pointing abscess. No probing during infection; DCR afterwards.
points: DDx: facial cellulitis (patent system), congenital dacryocystocele (bilateral → check airway), ethmoid sinusitis, frontal mucocele.
Gram-negative/atypical in diabetics, immunocompromised, nursing homes.
Topical alone inadequate; 10–14 days total.
CT if atypical, severe or not responding.
chunks.hook: Below the tendon = sac infection; above = suspect tumour.

cards.q: Why avoid probing in acute dacryocystitis?
cards.a: Risk of spreading infection/false passage; probe and irrigate after it settles.

chunks.title: Preseptal cellulitis
chunks.tldr: Red, hot, swollen lids but white eye, no proptosis, full painless motility, normal vision/pupils. Cause: abrasion, bite, hordeolum, dacryocystitis. Mild, >5 yrs, afebrile: oral co-amoxiclav / cefpodoxime (MRSA risk → TMP-SMX, doxy, clindamycin) 10–14 days. Admit for IV (vancomycin + ampicillin-sulbactam/ceftriaxone etc.) if toxic, ≤5 yrs, unreliable, or not better in 24–48 h.
points: DDx: orbital cellulitis, chalazion, allergy, erysipelas, necrotising fasciitis (grey-purple numb skin, septic → emergency debridement), viral conjunctivitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, HSV/VZV.
Non-immunised child → H. influenzae.
Bite/foul discharge → anaerobes.
CT orbit/sinuses if trauma, FB, orbital signs, abscess, no improvement.
MRSA risk factors: prior MRSA, contacts, healthcare stay, dialysis, IVDU, prison, contact sports.
Drain fluctuant abscess; consider steroids once covered.
chunks.hook: Swollen lid + quiet eye = preseptal. Proptosis/painful moves = orbital.

cards.q: Signs that distinguish orbital from preseptal cellulitis?
cards.a: Proptosis, painful/restricted eye movements, reduced vision, RAPD, chemosis.

cards.q: Children of what age with preseptal cellulitis are usually admitted?

chunks.title: Benign lid lesions
chunks.tldr: Seborrhoeic keratosis (stuck-on brown), cysts, molluscum (umbilicated, kids/HIV), naevus, xanthelasma (<40 yrs → lipids), squamous papilloma, actinic keratosis (premalignant, scaly). Malignant clues: ulceration, lash loss (madarosis), poliosis, distorted margin, bleeding, telangiectasia.
points: Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (myeloma) mimics xanthelasma.
Chronic contact dermatitis can mimic malignancy.
Diplopia/ophthalmoplegia = orbital invasion.
chunks.hook: Lost lashes over a lump = malignant until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Which patients with xanthelasma need a lipid profile?

chunks.title: Malignant lid tumours
chunks.tldr: BCC (commonest, lower lid/medial canthus; nodular with telangiectasia/ulcer, or morpheaform) → excision with margin control (Mohs/frozen); vismodegib if unresectable. SCC (perineural, nodal spread; from actinic keratosis). Keratoacanthoma (crater with keratin = low-grade SCC). Sebaceous carcinoma (elderly women, upper lid, mimics chalazion/blepharitis, pagetoid spread, prior radiation). Others: melanoma, Merkel, lymphoma, mets.
points: Palpate preauricular/submandibular/cervical nodes.
Incisional biopsy before big surgery; sentinel node for melanoma/sebaceous.
Lymphoma: send fresh tissue (flow cytometry).
SCC second-line: radiotherapy; imiquimod/interferon for non-surgical.
Sun protection advice.
